295.title: Patanjali 1.1–1.16: "now, yoga"; yoga is the stilling of the mind's turnings; practice and non-attachment (1 of 7)
295.hook: the most famous book about yoga opens with one word, and the word is now
295.tomorrow: Patanjali 1.2: the stilling of the mind's turnings (2 of 7)
295.howItsDone: The Yoga Sutras are studied line by line with a teacher and a commentary, often chanted in Sanskrit first; many yoga schools, in India and around the world, open their study with the first sutra.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Dvaita and beyond closed: I want to taste sugar, not become sugar. Two, and the space between is love. Today a new week, and a new book. Day two hundred ninety-five.
screen: `TWO, AND THE SPACE BETWEEN IS LOVE.`

segments.voice: Think about how you start things. The gym, in January. The diet, on Monday. The meditation app, once work calms down. There's always a better time coming, and it's never quite this one. Now picture the most famous book ever written about yoga. Not the poses: the mind. It's about two thousand years old, give or take a few centuries, and it has shaped nearly every serious yoga teacher since. You might expect it to open with a warning, or a promise, or a long list of what you need first. It opens with one word. And the word is now.
screen: `MONDAY. JANUARY. WHEN THINGS CALM DOWN.` → `THE BOOK OF YOGA.` → `ITS FIRST WORD: NOW.`

segments.voice: The book is the Yoga Sutras of Patanjali. A sutra is a thread: a short line, packed tight, meant to be memorized and then unpacked by a teacher. There are about a hundred and ninety-five of them, in four chapters. Who was Patanjali? Honestly, we don't know much. Scholars' guesses for the text span centuries, from about twenty-two hundred years ago to about fifteen hundred. Tradition tells beautiful stories about him, including that he was an incarnation of the great serpent who holds up the world. The first thread, in Sanskrit, is atha yoga anushasanam. Now, the teaching of yoga. Atha, now. It's a word Sanskrit books often start with. The Brahma Sutras open the same way: now, therefore, the inquiry into Brahman. Traditionally the word is also considered auspicious, a good sound to begin with. The oldest commentary on the Yoga Sutras says atha marks a beginning: here the teaching starts. But teachers have always found more in it. Now means the preparation is over. Now means you've arrived with whatever brought you here, a restless mind, a bad week, curiosity. Now means yoga isn't something that happens after your life gets sorted out. It's the sorting. This week we'll walk the first sixteen threads, slowly. Tomorrow, the famous definition of what yoga actually is. Today, just the first word. Everything the book will teach, it teaches to someone who has already begun.
screen: `A SUTRA IS A THREAD.` · `WHO WAS PATANJALI? WE DON'T KNOW MUCH.` · `ATHA: NOW, THE TEACHING BEGINS.` · `YOGA ISN'T AFTER YOUR LIFE. IT'S THE SORTING.` · then, large: `ATHA YOGĀNUŚĀSANAM.`

segments.voice: Sit exactly as you are. Don't fix your posture first, don't wait for the room to be quiet. Now. Notice what's here: the sound nearest to you, the feeling in your hands, the mood you brought in. Whenever your mind leaves for later or for earlier, say the word to yourself, gently: now. And come back. That's all. You'll probably say it many times. Every time counts as starting. If you pray, you can offer this now to God. The bell holds the time.
Patanjali 1.1. Atha yoga anushasanam: now, the teaching of yoga. The first thread of the Yoga Sutras, and the first word is now.
Your line: now. Today, pick one thing you've been saving for a better time, and give it five minutes. Now. Day two hundred ninety-five.

296.title: Patanjali 1.1–1.16: "now, yoga"; yoga is the stilling of the mind's turnings; practice and non-attachment (2 of 7)
296.hook: the whole definition of yoga, in four Sanskrit words, and not one of them is about stretching
296.tomorrow: Patanjali 1.3–1.4: the seer rests in itself (3 of 7)
296.howItsDone: Students of the Yoga Sutras often memorize 1.2 in Sanskrit, and many yoga teachers in India and abroad quote it as the definition of yoga before teaching any posture.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Patanjali 1.1: atha, now. The book of yoga begins with someone who has already begun. Your line was now. Did you start the thing you'd been saving? Day two hundred ninety-six.

Ask ten people what yoga is and you'll hear: stretching, a class at the gym, a mat, a pose with a funny name. Fair enough. That's what the word means on a lot of streets. Now open the Yoga Sutras to the second line, the one where Patanjali actually defines the word. Four Sanskrit words. Not one of them is about the body. Not one mentions breath, or posture, or flexibility. They're about something you carry everywhere, something that's been running since you woke up this morning, and is running right now, as you listen.
screen: `STRETCHING. A MAT. A POSE.` → `THE SECOND LINE.` → `FOUR WORDS, NONE ABOUT THE BODY.`

segments.voice: Here it is: yogash chitta vritti nirodhah. Yoga is the stilling of the turnings of the mind. Take it word by word. Chitta is the mind in the widest sense: thinking, feeling, remembering, the whole inner stuff. Vritti means a turning, a whirl, a movement, from a root that means to turn, like a wheel. Those are the thoughts, but also the moods, the memories, the half-conscious commentary: she didn't text back, I'm hungry, what was that song. And nirodha means stilling, restraining, bringing to rest. So yoga, for Patanjali, is what happens when the whirling settles. Teachers have always reached for the same picture here. Vivekananda, in his lectures on this book, used a lake. When the wind blows, the surface is covered in ripples, and you can't see the bottom. When the water goes still, you can see all the way down. Notice what the definition doesn't say. It doesn't say yoga is having no thoughts, or emptying your head by force. The word is stilling, like a pond settling, not like slamming a lid. And it doesn't say the ripples are bad. They're just ripples. Also notice how short it is. The whole rest of the book, all those threads, is really an unpacking of this one line: what the turnings are, why they won't settle, and how, slowly, they do. So when someone says they're bad at yoga because they can't touch their toes, Patanjali would have a gentle surprise for them.
screen: `YOGAŚ CITTA-VṚTTI-NIRODHAḤ.` · `CHITTA, VRITTI, NIRODHA: MIND, TURNING, STILL.` · `A LAKE WITH NO WIND.` · `STILLING, NOT SLAMMING A LID.` · then, large: `YOGA IS THE STILLING OF THE MIND'S TURNINGS.`

segments.voice: Sit, and picture a lake in the morning. There's a little wind on it. That's your mind right now. Don't try to stop the wind. Just watch the ripples: a thought, a sound, a small worry, each one a turning. Let each one pass across the surface and go. Breathe slowly, and notice that between the ripples, sometimes, the water is flat for a moment. Rest there when it comes. If you pray, you can let that stillness be your prayer. The bell holds the time.
Patanjali 1.1, and the thread right after it, 1.2: yoga is the stilling of the mind's turnings. Chitta, vritti, nirodha. Mind, turning, stillness.
Your line: now. Today, when the mind starts whirling, at a red light or a loading screen, catch one turning and let it settle. Now. Day two hundred ninety-six.

297.title: Patanjali 1.1–1.16: "now, yoga"; yoga is the stilling of the mind's turnings; practice and non-attachment (3 of 7)
297.hook: when the lake goes still, who is it that's looking?
297.howItsDone: In classical yoga study, sutras 1.3 and 1.4 are read with the Samkhya distinction between purusha, the seer, and prakriti, the seen, and meditation is described as learning to witness the mind rather than be swept along by it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Patanjali 1.2: yoga is the stilling of the mind's turnings. Chitta, vritti, nirodha. The lake going still. Did you catch a turning and let it settle? Your line is still now. Day two hundred ninety-seven.

You've had this happen. You're furious about something, an email, a comment, and for twenty minutes you are the anger. There's no you and the anger. There's just anger, wearing your face, typing the reply. Then something shifts. Maybe you take a walk, maybe you sleep on it, and suddenly you can see the anger, like weather passing over a field. It's there. But you're not it anymore. Something in you was watching the whole time. Patanjali's next two threads are about exactly that something.
screen: `YOU ARE THE ANGER.` → `THEN YOU CAN SEE IT.` → `SOMETHING WAS WATCHING.`

segments.voice: Thread three: then the seer rests in its own nature. In Sanskrit, tada drashtuh svarupe avasthanam. Tada, then: when the turnings have stilled. Drashta, the seer, the one who sees. Svarupa, its own form, its own true shape. When the lake is still, the seer simply is what it is. And thread four says what happens the rest of the time: otherwise, the seer takes on the form of the turnings. Vritti sarupyam itaratra. In plain words: most of the time, you look exactly like your thoughts. The anger arrives, and you become angry. The worry arrives, and you become worried. The old commentaries use a lovely picture. Put a clear crystal next to a red flower, and the crystal looks red. It isn't red. It never was. It's just sitting next to something red. So who is the seer? Here Patanjali leans on an older Hindu philosophy called Samkhya, which divides everything into two: the seer, called purusha, pure awareness, and everything that's seen, called prakriti, which includes the body, and, surprisingly, the mind itself. Thoughts are part of what's seen, not the one seeing. That's a strange idea the first time you hear it. Your thoughts are scenery. Different schools of Hindu thought describe the seer differently, and we met some of those debates in the last two weeks. But on this point they sound alike: you are not your weather.
screen: `TADĀ DRAṢṬUḤ SVARŪPE 'VASTHĀNAM.` · `OTHERWISE, IT LOOKS LIKE ITS THOUGHTS.` · `A CRYSTAL NEXT TO A RED FLOWER.` · `THOUGHTS ARE SEEN, NOT THE SEER.` · then, large: `YOU ARE NOT YOUR WEATHER.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let a thought come. Any thought. Instead of following it, notice it, the way you'd notice a car going by. There goes a thought. Then another. Each time, gently step back half a step: there's the thought, and here is the one seeing it. You don't have to name the seer or explain it. Just notice that noticing is happening, and that it isn't going anywhere. If you pray, you can rest in that quiet as a prayer. The bell holds the time.
Patanjali 1.1, with threads three and four: when the turnings still, the seer rests in its own nature. Otherwise it takes the shape of its thoughts.
Your line: now. Today, the next time a strong feeling arrives, say to yourself: a feeling is here, and I can see it. Now. Day two hundred ninety-seven.

298.title: Patanjali 1.1–1.16: "now, yoga"; yoga is the stilling of the mind's turnings; practice and non-attachment (4 of 7)
298.hook: Patanjali sorts every thought you'll ever have into five kinds, and one of them is sleep
298.howItsDone: Students of the Yoga Sutras often learn the five vrittis as a list and use them in meditation, noting which kind of thought is arising rather than following it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Patanjali 1.3 and 1.4: when the turnings still, the seer rests in itself; otherwise it looks like its thoughts. A crystal next to a red flower. Your line: now. Day two hundred ninety-eight.

Try to count your thoughts from this morning. You can't, of course. Hundreds, maybe thousands: the coffee, the weather, a face from high school, an argument you haven't had yet. It feels like chaos. Patanjali looked at that same chaos about two thousand years ago and did something very calm. He sorted it. Every turning of the mind, he says, fits into one of five kinds. Five drawers for everything you'll ever think. And the surprising part: one of the drawers is labeled sleep.
screen: `THOUSANDS OF THOUGHTS.` → `FIVE DRAWERS.` → `ONE IS LABELED SLEEP.`

segments.voice: Thread five says the turnings are five, and some bring pain and some don't. Then thread six lists them. First, right knowing: seeing what's actually there, reasoning well from it, or trusting a reliable witness. Second, error: knowing something that isn't so. The classic example is one you know from Advaita: the rope in the dusk that you take for a snake. Third, a slippery one: imagination, or knowledge from words alone. Patanjali means ideas that have no real object behind them. The commentators' example is the horn of a hare. You understand the phrase. There's no such thing. Fourth, sleep. That's the surprise. Deep sleep, Patanjali says, is still a turning of the mind, one that rests on absence, on nothing. The proof, the commentators say, is that you wake up and remember: I slept well. Something was there to know it. And fifth, memory: holding on to what you've already experienced. Now here's why the list matters. Once you can name a turning, it has less grip. It's not the truth arriving. It's a memory. It's an imagined scene. It's the rope again. And notice thread five: some turnings bring pain and some don't. Patanjali isn't asking you to hate your thoughts. Right knowing is a turning too, and a helpful one. The work of yoga is to know which drawer you're in, and in the end, to let all five go quiet.
screen: `PRAMĀṆA-VIPARYAYA-VIKALPA-NIDRĀ-SMṚTAYAḤ.` · `RIGHT KNOWING, ERROR, IMAGINATION.` · `SLEEP, AND MEMORY.` · `NAME THE TURNING; IT LOSES ITS GRIP.` · then, large: `FIVE DRAWERS FOR EVERY THOUGHT.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let the mind do what it does. When a thought comes, give it a drawer, softly. Memory. Imagination. Knowing. Error, maybe. If you drift toward drowsiness, you can even say: sleep. You don't need to be right about the drawer. The labeling is the practice. Label, and let it go, and wait for the next one. Every so often, notice the quiet between labels. If you pray, you can rest in that quiet. The bell holds the time.
Patanjali 1.1, and threads five to eleven: the five turnings. Right knowing, error, imagination, sleep and memory.
Your line: now. Today, when a worry shows up, ask which drawer it belongs in. Knowing? Or imagination? Then come back to now. Day two hundred ninety-eight.

299.title: Patanjali 1.1–1.16: "now, yoga"; yoga is the stilling of the mind's turnings; practice and non-attachment (5 of 7)
299.hook: the whole method of yoga in two words, and Krishna said the same two words to Arjuna
299.tomorrow: Patanjali 1.13–1.14: practice, over a long time (6 of 7)
299.howItsDone: Hindu teachers of meditation often pair abhyasa and vairagya, citing both Yoga Sutra 1.12 and Bhagavad Gita 6.35, and describe daily practice as returning again and again without clinging to results.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Patanjali 1.1 and on: the five turnings. Right knowing, error, imagination, sleep, memory. Did a worry turn out to be imagination? Your line: now. Day two hundred ninety-nine.

Remember Arjuna in the Gita, a few months ago on this path? Somewhere in the sixth chapter he stops Krishna and says, more or less: this is all beautiful, but my mind is restless. Holding it still is like holding the wind. Anyone who has tried to meditate for five minutes knows the feeling. Krishna doesn't argue. He agrees: yes, the mind is hard to hold. And then he gives two words for how it's done. Patanjali, in thread twelve, gives the very same two.
screen: `ARJUNA: MY MIND IS LIKE THE WIND.` → `KRISHNA AGREES.` → `TWO WORDS.`

segments.voice: Thread twelve: abhyasa vairagyabhyam tan nirodhah. By practice and non-attachment, they are stilled. They, meaning the turnings. Two words carry the whole method. Abhyasa, practice: coming back, again and again, to the thing you've chosen. Vairagya, non-attachment: letting go of the pull. Literally it means without coloring, without the red flower staining the crystal. Teachers often say the two are like the two wings of a bird. One wing alone, and you fly in circles. Practice without letting go becomes grinding: you sit every day, jaw clenched, demanding results. Letting go without practice becomes drifting: you're very relaxed and nothing changes. You need both. Coming back, and not clutching. And here is the Gita's answer to Arjuna, in the sixth chapter: the mind is restless, hard to hold, but it can be held by practice and by dispassion. The same pair, in the same order. Two great texts, from different schools, agree on the method. Now make it small. Practice is the phone you put face down again. Non-attachment is not caring, for a moment, whether it buzzes. Practice is returning to the breath. Non-attachment is not needing the breath to feel special. Tomorrow and the day after, Patanjali takes each wing on its own. Today, just notice that you need two.
screen: `ABHYĀSA-VAIRĀGYĀBHYĀṀ TAN-NIRODHAḤ.` · `ABHYASA: COMING BACK, AGAIN AND AGAIN.` · `VAIRAGYA: LETTING GO OF THE PULL.` · `TWO WINGS OF ONE BIRD.` · then, large: `PRACTICE, AND LET GO.`

segments.voice: Sit, and choose one thing to return to: the breath at the nose, or a word, or the sound of the room. That's the first wing. When the mind wanders, and it will, come back. Don't scold it. That's the second wing: no clutching, no scorekeeping. Come back, let go, come back, let go. The rhythm of it is the whole method, small. If you pray, the thing you return to can be a name of God. The bell holds the time.
Patanjali 1.1, and thread twelve: by practice and non-attachment, the turnings are stilled. Abhyasa and vairagya. Two wings.
Your line: now. Today, pick one small thing to come back to every time you get distracted, and let go of how well you're doing it. Day two hundred ninety-nine.

300.title: Patanjali 1.1–1.16: "now, yoga"; yoga is the stilling of the mind's turnings; practice and non-attachment (6 of 7)
300.hook: day three hundred, and Patanjali's three conditions for a practice that holds
300.howItsDone: Teachers of the Yoga Sutras often cite 1.14 to explain why daily practice matters more than intensity: a practice kept over a long time, steadily and with respect, becomes firmly grounded.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Patanjali 1.12: practice and non-attachment, the two wings. Did you find one small thing to come back to? Your line: now. Today, the first wing up close. Day three hundred.

Three hundred days. Pause on that for a second. Three hundred times, give or take, you've opened this and sat for a few minutes. Some days it probably felt like something. Some days it felt like nothing at all, like brushing your teeth. Here's a question worth asking on a day like this: what makes a practice actually hold? Not for a week of enthusiasm, but for years? Patanjali, who was clearly writing for people who struggle, gives three conditions in one line.
screen: `THREE HUNDRED DAYS.` → `SOME DAYS, NOTHING AT ALL.` → `WHAT MAKES A PRACTICE HOLD?`

segments.voice: First, thread thirteen defines practice. Abhyasa is the effort to stay there: to remain steady in that stillness. Not the stillness itself, notice. The effort. The returning. Practice is the coming back, which means every time you drift and return, that isn't failure. That's the practice happening. Then thread fourteen: it becomes firmly grounded when it's attended to for a long time, without interruption, and with devotion. Three conditions. A long time: dirgha kala. Not a weekend retreat. Seasons. Years. Without break: nairantarya. The commentators mean steadiness, a thread that keeps running. Teachers who know real lives read it kindly: not perfection, but a practice that doesn't wait for ideal conditions. And with devotion: satkara. That word means doing something with respect, with care, as if it matters. The same practice done carelessly and done with care are not the same practice. And what's the result? Dridha bhumi. Firm ground. Like soil that's been walked on so many times it becomes a path you can stand on in a storm. Here's the quiet good news in this line. Patanjali doesn't say you'll feel peaceful every day. He doesn't promise fireworks. He promises ground. Long time, steady, with care, and one day you notice you have somewhere to stand. Three hundred days is a real start on the first condition.
screen: `PRACTICE IS THE EFFORT TO RETURN.` · `A LONG TIME, WITHOUT BREAK.` · `AND WITH DEVOTION: SATKARA.` · `THE RESULT: FIRM GROUND.` · then, large: `SA TU DĪRGHA-KĀLA-NAIRANTARYA-SATKĀRĀSEVITO DṚḌHA-BHŪMIḤ.`

segments.voice: Sit, and treat these two minutes with a little extra care. Straighten your back as if someone you respect were in the room. Breathe in slowly, all the way. Breathe out slowly, all the way. When you drift, come back, and count the coming back as the practice, not the drifting as a failure. Nothing needs to happen. You're laying ground. If you pray, you can offer these three hundred days to God, the ordinary ones most of all. The bell holds the time.
Patanjali 1.1, and threads thirteen and fourteen: practice is the effort to return, and it becomes firm ground over a long time, steadily, with care.
Your line: now. Today, do one ordinary thing you do every day, a dish, a commute, a bedtime story, with satkara: real care, as if it matters. Day three hundred.

301.title: Patanjali 1.1–1.16: "now, yoga"; yoga is the stilling of the mind's turnings; practice and non-attachment (7 of 7)
301.hook: letting go of what you've seen, and of what you've only heard about, and then a letting go beyond that
301.tomorrow: the lineage tracks begin: karma, bhakti, jnana
301.howItsDone: In Hindu teaching, vairagya is not only for monks: householders are taught to hold wealth, family and even religious rewards loosely, and the Yoga Sutras' opening chapter is often studied as a complete short course in meditation.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Patanjali 1.14: a long time, without break, with care, and practice becomes firm ground. Three hundred days. Your line: now. Today, the other wing, and the week closes. Day three hundred one.

Some things pull at you because you've tasted them. The last slice of cake. The ping of a new message. The feeling of being right in an argument. And some things pull at you because you've only heard about them. The trip everyone posts about. The life your cousin seems to have. The perfect calm that serious meditators supposedly reach. Patanjali noticed both kinds of pull, and he named them in the same breath. Then he went one step further, to a letting go that most of us have never even imagined.
screen: `WHAT YOU'VE TASTED.` → `WHAT YOU'VE ONLY HEARD ABOUT.` → `ONE STEP FURTHER.`

segments.voice: Thread fifteen: non-attachment is the mastery of one who no longer thirsts for things seen, or things heard about. Seen means this world: the cake, the praise, the paycheck. Heard about means everything promised by tradition or rumor, and the old commentators include heavenly rewards here too. Even spiritual prizes can become one more thing to crave. The word Patanjali uses for the result is vashikara: mastery, being in charge of the pull rather than pulled by it. Notice he doesn't say the cake disappears. You can still eat the cake. It just doesn't own you. Then thread sixteen, the higher kind: from knowing the seer, the purusha, comes freedom from thirst even for the gunas, the basic strands that make up everything in nature. That's a letting go at the root. Not just of this craving or that one, but of the whole weave, because you've seen what you are underneath it. Now look back at the whole week. Thread one: now. Thread two: yoga is the stilling of the mind's turnings. Three and four: the seer resting in itself, or looking like its thoughts, a crystal beside a red flower. Five to eleven: the five turnings, sleep among them. Twelve: two wings, practice and letting go. Thirteen and fourteen: the long, steady, careful practice that becomes firm ground. And today, fifteen and sixteen: letting go of what you've tasted and what you've heard of, and at last, of the thirst itself. Sixteen threads. One week. A whole way of life, and it started with now.
screen: `NO THIRST FOR THINGS SEEN OR HEARD OF.` · `VASHIKARA: MASTERY OF THE PULL.` · `THE HIGHER KIND: FREE AT THE ROOT.` · `SIXTEEN THREADS, ONE WEEK.` · then, large: `TAT PARAṀ PURUṢA-KHYĀTER GUṆA-VAITṚṢṆYAM.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let one pull come to mind. Something you've tasted and want again, or something you've only heard about and want anyway. Hold it gently. Notice where you feel it: the chest, the stomach, the hands. Breathe into that place. You don't have to give the thing up. Just loosen your grip on it by one finger, then another. Feel what it's like to want something and not be owned by it. If you pray, you can offer the wanting to God. The bell holds the time.
Patanjali 1.1, and all sixteen threads to 1.16: now, the stilling of the turnings, practice and letting go, all the way down to the root.
Your line: now. Today, when something pulls at you, enjoy it or don't, but loosen your grip by one finger. Now. Day three hundred one.
